In convex integration, the oscillations are typically built by hand and the iteration procedure creates wild weak solutions. The non-uniqueness construction of Albritton–Brué–Colombo used an unstable vortex to split solutions apart. The Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa singularities amplify vorticity across scales by strain. In the openAI paper, a fluid instability is clever made so that the flow itself generates the oscillations: they grow by drawing energy from the background shear. The Reynolds stress then becomes the force that creates the collapsing smooth vortex. Using a physical instability to create the stress in this way has no precedent, and it is what produces a smooth force rather than a merely rough one. Some on these ideas are in the literature (e.g. Leibovich-Stewartson 1983) but the way they are combined is definitely insane and definitely nowhere in the literature previously. I also don't know of anyone suggesting that convex integration would play a role in the creation of a blow-up solution like this. On a technical level, the paper is unbelievable, maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding: there are several different groups of pde experts working on understanding it who say that they more or less understand now. we've found and have been working on disclosure for a remote code execution in a widely-deployed compression library. it's both an impactful issue and an example that shows how complicated it can be to coordinate patching, since it's integrated into a lot of downstream software: OpenAI (@OpenAI) During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy. The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server. This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE. More details on the patch and mitigations below: patchtheplanet.org/brotli Link Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) — Patch the Planet Brotli decoder vulnerability: affected software, fixed releases, and how to disable Brotli decoding while you patch. patchtheplanet.org — https://nitter.kareem.one/OpenAI/status/2113766354386084338#m

A post on how we've been securing our frontier model training environment. We've been building tools around our frontier cyber models, which have secured us far beyond what we could have unassisted and should generalize as key to how defenders secure themselves going forward. OpenAI (@OpenAI) Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications. On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments. While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software. After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely. openai.com/index/securing-ou… Link Securing our frontier model training environment OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming. openai.com — https://nitter.kareem.one/OpenAI/status/2113718797505036665#m

I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus. The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future. I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf. Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent. Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade. Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine. Why now We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. Believing before consensus My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine. I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today. I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?” Then we work backward together to make it happen. In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI , before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue. In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models. In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point. The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale. @linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike. @tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues. @Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies. Making the ambition possible Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight. These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work. This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger. Thank you To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together. Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me. To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap. Let’s get to work!

Une faille de sécurité informatique inconnue des développeurs, et donc sans correctif immédiat, la rendant très dangereuse.
La capacité d'une IA à agir de manière autonome pour accomplir des tâches complexes, en prenant des initiatives et en gérant des étapes multiples.
Lorsque les paramètres internes d'un modèle d'IA sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de l'étudier, de l'utiliser ou de le modifier.
La quantité d'informations (mots, caractères) qu'un modèle d'IA peut 'retenir' et prendre en compte à la fois pour comprendre et générer du texte.

highlights.text_fr: Un article sur la manière dont nous avons sécurisé notre environnement d'entraînement des modèles de pointe. Le 20 septembre, après qu'un modèle a exploité une mauvaise configuration DNS pour trouver un moyen de sortir de ce monde hors ligne, nous avons interrompu l'entraînement des modèles de pointe pour renforcer davantage le confinement. Nous avons assemblé des équipes d'agents, alimentées par nos modèles les plus performants en cyber-sécurité, et les avons chargées de trouver des faiblesses dans nos environnements de recherche. Bien qu'ils n'aient trouvé aucune route vers Internet qu'ils auraient pu facilement exploiter tout en dissimulant leur activité à nos moniteurs, ils ont découvert des vulnérabilités "zero-day", des évasions de machines virtuelles et des canaux secondaires matériels pour la communication entre agents. Nous avons utilisé leurs découvertes pour renforcer encore nos défenses et apporter des correctifs aux logiciels open source. Après avoir renforcé notre architecture de confinement, nous avons repris l'entraînement et l'inférence de nos modèles de pointe en apprentissage par renforcement le 1er octobre. idees.text_fr: Au niveau technique, l'article est incroyable, peut-être au-delà de ce qu'un humain aurait pu concevoir, mais pas au-delà de la compréhension humaine", dit Scott Armstrong (@scottnarmstrong). Étant bloqué pour répondre à ce fil, je réponds ici en citant le tweet : la construction d'OpenAI s'apparente davantage à l'intégration convexe qu'à autre chose. Dans l'intégration convexe, les oscillations sont généralement construites à la main et le processus itératif crée des solutions faibles "sauvages". La construction de non-unicité d'Albritton–Brué–Colombo utilisait un vortex instable pour séparer les solutions. Les singularités de Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa amplifient la vorticité à travers les échelles par la contrainte. Dans l'article d'OpenAI, une instabilité fluide est intelligemment utilisée pour que l'écoulement lui-même génère les oscillations : elles se développent en puisant de l'énergie dans le cisaillement de fond. La contrainte de Reynolds devient alors la force qui crée le vortex lisse en effondrement. L'utilisation d'une instabilité physique pour créer la contrainte de cette manière est sans précédent, et c'est ce qui produit une force lisse plutôt qu'une simple force brute. Certaines de ces idées existent dans la littérature (par exemple, Leibovich-Stewartson 1983), mais la façon dont elles sont combinées est vraiment incroyable et n'a jamais été vue auparavant. Je ne connais personne non plus qui ait suggéré que l'intégration convexe jouerait un rôle dans la création d'une solution d'explosion comme celle-ci. Techniquement, l'article est incroyable, peut-être au-delà de ce qu'un humain aurait pu concevoir, mais pas au-delà de la compréhension humaine : plusieurs groupes d'experts en équations aux dérivées partielles (EDP) travaillent à le comprendre et disent qu'ils le saisissent plus ou moins maintenant. Je m'attends à des synthèses bientôt. Pour résumer : quiconque dit que ce résultat d'OpenAI n'est pas surprenant ment, désolé !

In convex integration, the oscillations are typically built by hand and the iteration procedure creates wild weak solutions. The non-uniqueness construction of Albritton–Brué–Colombo used an unstable vortex to split solutions apart. The Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa singularities amplify vorticity across scales by strain. In the openAI paper, a fluid instability is clever made so that the flow itself generates the oscillations: they grow by drawing energy from the background shear. The Reynolds stress then becomes the force that creates the collapsing smooth vortex. Using a physical instability to create the stress in this way has no precedent, and it is what produces a smooth force rather than a merely rough one. Some on these ideas are in the literature (e.g. Leibovich-Stewartson 1983) but the way they are combined is definitely insane and definitely nowhere in the literature previously. I also don't know of anyone suggesting that convex integration would play a role in the creation of a blow-up solution like this. On a technical level, the paper is unbelievable, maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding: there are several different groups of pde experts working on understanding it who say that they more or less understand now.
